findings.description: The `section_terminator` regex (line 80–85) requires `\s*:` immediately after the section keyword. The alternation includes `FIND` which is a 4-character token. In finding text where a model writes `FINDINGS:` (plural) or `FINDER:` as a subsection label, the regex would NOT match (`FIND` matches but the next char `I`/`E` isn't `\s` or `:`). This is correct. However, the regex DOES match `FIND :` (space before colon) because `\s*:` allows intervening whitespace. The actual gap is: the alternation lacks `ALTERNATIVE` and `DIVERGENCE` (§18 divergence directive headers), `FEEDBACK` (§17), and `RESUBMISSION`. If any of these appear as section headers after an ADMISSIBILITY block, the terminator won't fire and the admissibility block will over-extend into unrelated content, polluting gate-status matches.

The `parse_admissibility_block` function returns `list(ADMISSIBILITY_GATES)` (all five gates) when `finding_text` is empty OR when the ADMISSIBILITY marker is not found. These two cases are semantically distinct: (1) the finding text is empty (no finding submitted at all), vs (2) the finding text exists but lacks an ADMISSIBILITY block (the model forgot to include it). FIND: The `section_terminator` regex at lines 80-85 includes `FINDING_ID` and `FINDING` as alternations, but the alternation order places `FINDING_ID` before `FINDING`. While the regex engine backtracks and this is functionally correct (as noted in the code comment), there is a subtle edge case: if a line contains "FINDING_ID:" followed by more text on the same line (e.g., "FINDING_ID: F007 (some note)"), the regex matches "FINDING_ID:" and the `start()` position is correct. However, if a line contains "FINDING:" followed by "_ID" (e.g., "FINDING:_ID: something" — malformed but possible), the regex would match "FINDING:" at the start, and the `start()` would be at "FINDING", truncating before "_ID: something". This is a minor edge case but could cause incorrect block termination if a model produces malformed output. More critically, the terminator regex uses `\s*:` which matches zero or more whitespace followed by a colon. If a line within the ADMISSIBILITY block contains a section keyword followed immediately by a colon without whitespace (e.g., "Note: finding_id is C0001"), the regex would match "finding_id:" (with case-insensitivity after F007 fix) and prematurely terminate. The `\s*` allows zero whitespace, so "finding_id:" matches even when it's part of a sentence. This is a false-positive risk.

FOLLOW: Premature termination causes the block to be truncated before all gate statuses are parsed. Gates after the false match are excluded, potentially causing false FAIL reports. The feedback channel then instructs models to fix gates that are actually PASS, wasting rounds and eroding trust in the corrective loop. This interacts with C0025 (premature termination on section keywords in rationale) — the zero-whitespace allowance makes the problem strictly worse.

ANALYSE: SOFT constraint — parser robustness. The `\s*` before the colon is intentionally permissive, but zero-width match creates unnecessary false positives. Premise 1: Section headers in the finding format are always followed by `: ` (colon-space) or `:\n` (colon-newline). Premise 2: The regex `\s*:` matches colon with zero or more whitespace, including zero. Premise 3: A line like "Note: finding_id is C0001" contains "finding_id:" with zero whitespace between "finding_id" and ":". Conclusion: The regex will match this as a section terminator, causing premature block termination. CONFIRMED by construction.

FIX: Require at least one whitespace character or end-of-line after the colon, or require that the colon be followed by whitespace or end-of-line. Change `\s*:` to `\s*:\s+` to require at least one whitespace after the colon, or `\s*:\s*$` to require the line to end after the colon. The simplest sufficient fix: change `\s*:` to `\s*:\s+` so the colon must be followed by at least one whitespace character (preventing match on "finding_id:" embedded in text where the colon is immediately followed by a word character). However, this would fail to match a section header at end-of-file with no trailing newline. Safer: use `\s*:\s*(?:$|\s)` to allow end-of-string or whitespace. But the simplest: `\s*:\s+` and also allow end-of-string by making the whitespace optional but with a word-boundary check.
